note: Short, sourced stories about names and where they travelled. Own words only; every paragraph cites claims, every claim cites a page with a quote that was found on it. Nothing about a person.

ellis-island-names.title: Was your family's name changed at Ellis Island?
ellis-island-names.dek: Almost never. The name on the ship's list was written in Europe before the voyage, and the changes that did happen came later, by choice, usually in a courtroom.

p.t: The National Archives and the National Park Service, which looks after Ellis Island, both say the same thing: immigration officers there were not authorised to change anyone's name, and the surviving records rarely support the story.
Names did change. They changed mostly by the immigrant's own choice, mostly after arrival, and the authors who studied this place most of those changes at naturalization, in front of a court.

sections.h: Who wrote the name down, and where

p.t: The passenger list, called the manifest, was prepared in Europe before the ship sailed, normally at the port of departure, by the shipping line's clerks. It was not made at Ellis Island.

The details usually reached the clerk through a ticket agent. For a prepaid ticket they often came from a relative already in the United States, not from the traveller. Sources name different hands for the compiling: the shipping line's clerks in one, the ship's purser in a study of South African departures.
Federal law has required the master of an arriving ship to hand over a passenger list since 1 January 1820.
At Ellis Island the manifest was the basis of inspection, the only official arrival record. Each passenger was given a numbered ticket that matched a page and line of it.

The inspectors did not write a list of names of their own. They examined each arrival, with a quick medical look and a Board of Special Inquiry for doubtful cases, against the list that had come with the ship. Where someone was held, the detention or special-inquiry papers should show the same name as the manifest line.

Ellis Island did employ interpreters, hired through a federal civil service examination that tested speaking, reading, writing and comprehension in each language. Many were immigrants or the children of immigrants, and the Park Service lists about two dozen languages, among them Italian, Yiddish, Greek, Arabic and Chinese.
Because the inspector was comparing a person to a list already written, the interpreter's job was to make that comparison possible, not to spell a name for the first time.

The belief that officials renamed arrivals is not found in popular writing for decades after the station's busiest years. It took hold in the 1970s. A film of 1974 showed an immigration officer giving a child a new name, and several sources name it as a major carrier of the story.

One historian's explanation of why it lasts: after the 1965 immigration law ended national-origin quotas, Ellis Island became a symbol of immigrant struggle; distrust of government in the 1970s made official wrongdoing believable; and blaming an official was easier than admitting that parents and grandparents had chosen new names themselves.

The law gave courts the power. The Naturalization Act of 29 June 1906 allowed state, territorial and federal courts of record, when someone was naturalised and on that person's own petition, to make a decree changing the name. The certificate was then issued in the new name. The present statute carries the same power.

So the paper trail is often in a court. Before 1906 any court of record, municipal, county, state or federal, could naturalise, in two steps: a declaration of intention ("first papers") and a petition ("second papers"). The 1906 Act made the forms uniform and required the petition to give the name of the vessel and the date and place of arrival.
Separate name-change petitions also exist in court records; the National Archives office in Chicago, for one, holds some for selected courts and periods.

The one official change a researcher found in the Ellis Island records ran the other way. A traveller admitted after a special inquiry had been listed under a false name, and the manifest was corrected to the legal name through the official process.

Most drift is copying. A name is copied from the ticket to the manifest, to an index, to naturalization papers, to a census, and each copy can alter it. Those who transcribe a manifest also misread handwriting, so one person can appear under different first-name forms across records.

Names were not a priority before 1911, when inspection focused on age, money, work and health. From 1911 the government paid more attention to the accuracy of names and shipping lines faced fines for careless manifests, and from 1917 and 1918 manifests were typed and prepared from passports.

sections.h: What to do when you search

p.t: Start with what family documents say: names, date and place of arrival, port of departure, age. Then the census, which from 1900 to 1930 gives a year of immigration, then the manifest, then the naturalization papers, using each to correct the last. Always try many spellings.

Search by more than the family spelling: the given name (the American form may differ from the one on the manifest), the age (often mistranscribed), the ship's name (naturalization papers sometimes name the wrong ship) and the nearest relative at home or in the United States. Use wildcard or sounds-like options, and look at the manifest page image, not only the index.
After mid-1924 most passengers were inspected at American consulates abroad instead of at Ellis Island, so for later arrivals the visa or consular record is part of the trail.
Ellis Island began receiving immigrants on 1 January 1892 and the station was abandoned or officially closed in 1954. Over those 62 years more than 12 million immigrants came through it.

The Park Service dates the station's largest and most active period as 1892 to 1924; the 1924 immigration law moved inspection to consulates, and Ellis Island went on to 1954 for detention and other purposes.
1907 was the busiest year, with more than a million immigrants processed.

italianisation-1927.title: Why a Slavic surname turns Italian in a register after 1927
italianisation-1927.dek: Around Trieste, Istria, Fiume and Zara, Italy changed surnames by decree from 1927. The decree was written in the margin of the birth entry, so the old and the new form can both be on the record.

p.t: The first instrument was not about the Adriatic at all. A royal decree-law of 10 January 1926 dealt with the families of the Province of Trento, which then included Alto Adige, and was converted into law that May. It was presented as the restitution of Italian forms of surnames.

Its first article applied to families whose original Italian or Latin surname had been translated, distorted by foreign spelling or given a foreign suffix; those families "resumed" the original form. A second article let a foreign surname be "reduced" to Italian form if its holder asked. Going on using the foreign form after restitution carried a fine of 500 to 5,000 lire.

A royal decree of 7 April 1927 (n. 494) extended these rules to the territories annexed after 1920 under the treaties with Austria and with Yugoslavia, which means the Venezia Giulia provinces. It was published on 22 April 1927 and has since been repealed in a clean-up of old laws.

Fiume came in separately. A decree of 31 May 1928 applied the same rules to the Fiume territory, so for Fiume the legal start is a year later than for Trieste, Gorizia and Pola. We did not find the instrument that brought in Zara, so this story does not date it.

The prefecture of each province started the change. Each used an advisory commission of philologists, linguists and jurists to decide which surnames counted as foreign and what Italian form they should take. Pola's commission finished first, in 1928, then Trieste's in 1929, then Gorizia, Udine, Fiume and Zara in 1930. The restitution or reduction was then made by a decree of the prefect. A person could ask, and the prefect could also act without being asked.

On paper the steps were: the decree was notified to the person concerned, published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale, copied into a special register and noted in the margin of the entry in the birth register. The civil-status code of 1939 confirmed all of this and forbade giving foreign first names to children who were Italian citizens.

The later restoration law names, as people who may ask to go back, not only those named in a decree but also the spouse and relatives to whom the surname "was extended", and their descendants registered under it. That wording suggests that a decree for one person was in practice carried across the household; it is our reading of the law's wording, not a rule the 1927 text is quoted as stating.

sections.h: The reason given, and the reality

p.t: The stated reason was restitution: many surnames of Latin or Italian origin, it was said, had been altered under Austrian rule, with Slavic priests and clerks adding endings or translating names. A legal scholar who reports this as the justification offered at the time then points out that the history was mixed. Habsburg municipal and parish offices converted surnames in both directions, often on request, by the sound and spelling the clerk used.

Slavic endings varied already under the Habsburgs and depended on who kept the register. Where offices were run by Slovenes or Croats, -ic was often added even to Latin, Italian or German surnames; where offices were Italian or Austro-German, the ending was usually kept but written -ich or -itsch. So a spelling in a register from before 1918 is not a fixed guide to a family's origin.

The sources describe four kinds of change: translating a surname from its Slavic or German form into Italian; dropping or reshaping a foreign suffix or spelling, above all the -ic or -ich ending; "restoring" a supposed original Latin or Italian form; and reducing a foreign-origin surname to Italian form on request. The examples a 1929 Trieste source gave of earlier alteration are pairs such as Bassi and Bassich, Fabiani and Fabianich (an ending added) and Bevilacqua and Vodopivez (a translation). Those are the claimed pre-1918 alterations the decrees said they were undoing, not examples of any particular family.

First names were treated by a different route. In 1923 the city of Trieste forbade registrars to enter Slavic first names in the birth register. A law of 1928 banned first names that were "ridiculous or shameful" or offended national sentiment, and let registrars act even on names already in use. An adult's first name could be changed when it was transcribed in registry paperwork, because a first name showed the mother tongue while a surname showed only origin. We found no source that gives pairs such as Ivan and Giovanni, so none is claimed here.

It was uneven. In the province of Udine the rules were applied more mildly, with no changes of Slovene surnames except on request. In Alto Adige changes happened almost always on request and reached no more than about 4,000 by 1939. The Fiume and Zara commissions finished in 1930, but their results were never made public.

Before the decree, changes were voluntary and used the Austrian law still in force, an imperial decree of 1826 that allowed changes in cases "worthy of particular regard". Until Italian civil registration arrived on 1 January 1924, a little over 300 changes were authorised in Trieste. Italian law then charged tax on name changes, which largely stopped the process until the free route of 1926 and 1927.

Between 1918 and 1922 about 1,000 people petitioned in a population of roughly 350,000 in Venezia Giulia, mostly in and around Trieste. The historian who counted them reads them as people choosing to show that they belonged in Italy.

The numbers for the decree years do not agree, and we do not choose between them. The Pola commission in 1928 listed more than 3,000 surnames to be Italianised and Trieste's in 1929 more than 2,000; these are committee lists, not decrees. In 1936 alone the Gazzetta published 4,332 decrees that renamed 18,098 people. One scholar thinks the overall total may have approached 50,000 changes. An estimate of 100,000 people changed in Trieste province alone, from 1919 to 1945, is judged exaggerated by the same scholar, while another account gives 3,000 surnames and 60,000 people for that province, and a third says "hundreds of thousands". The Gazzetta also did not publish every decree, so published counts are incomplete.

On the Yugoslav side, the assembly of Istrian representatives that met in September 1943 included among its decisions the change of forcibly Italianised surnames, names and place names. One author, writing from the point of view of the exiles, adds that after 1945 in the annexed territories Italianised names were restored at once, and that many ordinary Italian surnames were also reshaped into Slavic form, even for people who had left. That is one author's account and not a legal text.

On the Italian side the early steps were small. In 1945 the Interior Ministry directed that restoring original surnames be made easier, and a circular of 20 April 1946 let surnames Italianised on the holder's own request be brought back. In the Free Territory of Trieste the Allied Military Government ordered, in December 1947, free restoration of surnames in Slavic form on request, and after 1954 the Trieste prefecture was allowed to use the procedure set for Alto Adige. Very few of the people who could have applied did so in the climate of the Cold War.

Law 114 of 28 March 1991 recognises a right to restore the original form of a surname assumed or assigned under the 1926 decree. The people who may ask are those named in the decree, the spouse and relatives to whom the surname was extended, and descendants registered under it. They ask the prefecture that issued the decree, or the Prefecture of Trieste if that province is no longer in Italy. The procedure is free and has no time limit. The prefect revokes the old decree and restores the original form, the new decree is entered in the birth register and noted at the foot of the birth record, and other registers are corrected by the office. A law of 2001 allows restoration on other evidence where the original decree cannot be found.

A further law of 1999 lets members of recognised linguistic minorities, Slovene and Croatian among them, who live in the listed communes restore surnames or names changed before the law, including a baptismal first name they were prevented from giving in the minority language.

sections.h: What this means when you search

p.t: Both forms can exist in the records. Under the 1927 mechanism the birth entry was not rewritten; the decree is recorded in the margin. An entry from before the decree should therefore show the earlier form, with the later form noted at the side. Because decrees were extended across a household, a person, a spouse and children may carry the new form from different dates. The 2001 law itself names parish baptism certificates, and decrees issued for brothers or sisters, as acceptable evidence of the original form, which suggests parish records can keep the original.

Decrees were published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale del Regno, and researchers have worked from them. One analysed the decrees in detail with a case study of the Pola prefecture, and another published lists for Trieste, Gorizia and Istria with data on the first 5,300 cases. The Gazzetta did not print every decree.

Search for more than the family spelling. The changes mostly removed or reshaped a foreign suffix such as -ic or -ich, respelled foreign orthography, or translated the surname. So try the stem without the ending, the Italian-respelled form and a translated form, and, because an adult's first name could also be altered at transcription, expect the first name to differ too. This is our inference from the kinds of change described above, not a rule any source states.

What we could confirm is thin. The State Archives in Rijeka hold the Prefettura di Fiume fonds for 1922 to 1947, 188 books and 2,128 boxes, mostly cabinet and general files. The State Archive in Trieste holds a Prefettura di Trieste fonds, but the catalogue record we read describes only its 1938 to 1944 racial-law series. A guide to the Gorizia State Archive says it holds the prefecture's papers. None of these pages mentions the name-change decrees or registers, so whether the decree files are there has to be asked of each archive. The 1991 law sends requests to the issuing prefecture, or to Trieste if the province is no longer Italian, which suggests the Trieste prefecture is the first contact for Pola, Fiume and Zara.

i16.claim: Pre-fascist voluntary changes were small compared with the 1927-onwards decrees: Hametz's abstract reports about 1,000 petitioners from a population of roughly 350,000 in Venezia Giulia between 1918 and 1922, mostly from Trieste and its surroundings; she reads them as people choosing to show belonging in Italy.

i17.claim: Yugoslav side, 1943: the Assembly of Istrian People's Representatives (25-26 Sept 1943, the Pazin Decisions) included among its decisions the change of forcibly Italianised surnames, names and toponyms. After 1945, Troilo (citing Cernic and D'Alessio) says that in the territories annexed to Yugoslavia the Italianised surnames and names were restored at once, and that a large share of ordinary Italian surnames were also reshaped into Slavic form, even for people who had left, so exiles who asked local offices for papers sometimes found surnames, and often first names, changed. This last part is one author's account from the exile viewpoint, not a legal text.

i18.claim: Italian side, early steps: in 1945 the Interior Ministry directed that restoration of original surnames be made easier, and a Prime Minister's circular of 20 April 1946 allowed surnames Italianised on the holder's own request to be brought back to the original form on application to local authorities. In the Free Territory of Trieste the Allied Military Government ordered, in December 1947, free restoration of surnames in Slavic form on request. After Trieste returned to Italy (1954) the Interior Ministry let the Trieste prefecture use the procedure set for Alto Adige; a 24 June 1948 note had done the same for Gorizia. Uptake was small: very few of the potential applicants took it up in the Cold War climate.

i19.claim: Italian statute for the Adriatic provinces: Law 28 March 1991 n. 114 (GU 8 April 1991) recognises a right to restore the original form of the Italian surname assumed or assigned under RDL 17/1926. Who may ask: people named in the prefectural decree, the spouse and relatives to whom the surname was extended, and descendants registered under it. Where: the prefecture that issued the decree, or the Prefecture of Trieste if that province is no longer in Italy. Process: the prefect revokes the old decree and restores the original form; the procedure is free and has no time limit; the new decree is entered in the birth register and noted at the foot of the birth record, and other registers are corrected by the office. Law 38/2001 allows restoration on other documentation where the original decree cannot be found.

i20.claim: Broader Italian rights: Law 15 Dec 1999 n. 482 art. 11 lets members of recognised linguistic minorities (including Slovene and Croatian) living in the listed communes restore surnames or names changed before the law, and also those prevented from giving a baptismal first name in the minority language; the restoration of a surname also covers minor descendants (adult ones if they consent). Law 118/1972 had earlier provided a German-form route for Bolzano province only (a separate story).

i21.claim: Both forms exist in records. Under the 1927 mechanism the birth entry is not rewritten: the decree is recorded in the margin, so a birth register entry from before the decree should show the earlier form with the later form noted at the side. Since decrees extended to spouse and relatives, siblings, a spouse and children may carry the new form from different dates. Law 38/2001 itself names parish baptism certificates, and decrees issued for brothers or sisters, as acceptable evidence of the original form, which implies parish records can retain the original form.

i22.claim: Decrees were published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale del Regno (4,332 in 1936 alone), and scholars have worked from them: Cereghetti Passini analyses the Gazzetta decrees with a close case study of the Pola (Istria) prefecture; Parovel (1985) published lists for Trieste, Gorizia and Istria with data on the first 5,300 cases. Cereghetti warns the Gazzetta did not publish every decree.

i23.claim: Archives (what the fetched pages actually support): the Rijeka State Archives hold the fonds 'Riječka prefektura' (Prefettura di Fiume), 1922-1947, 188 books and 2,128 boxes, mostly cabinet and general files. The Trieste State Archive holds a Prefettura di Trieste fonds, but the EHRI record describes only the 1938-44 racial-law series. The State Archive of Gorizia is described by a Coronini-foundation guide as holding the Prefettura and Questura di Gorizia among Italian-state offices from the 1920s. None of these pages mentions the name-change decrees or registers specifically, so whether the decree files sit in these fonds must be checked with each archive. The 1991 law routes requests to the issuing prefecture, or to Trieste if the province is no longer Italian, which suggests the Trieste prefecture is the contact point for Pola, Fiume and Zara cases.

i24.claim: Searching for the Italianised form: the sources say the changes mostly (a) removed or reshaped a foreign suffix such as -ic/-ich, (b) respelled foreign orthography, or (c) translated the surname. So a search for a Slavic or German name in post-1927 civil records should include the stem without the suffix, the Italian-respelled form, and a translated form; and, because adults' first names could also be altered at transcription, the first name may differ too. These pointers follow from the types described by Troilo (art. 1 'suffisso straniero', translation examples) and are an editorial inference, not a rule any source states.
